name: Nandan Nilekani
role: Infosys cofounder and former chair of India’s Unique Identification Authority
summary: Nilekani favours competitive markets within public rules, technology-built public platforms for welfare and identity, and democratic, decentralised government with empowered cities. He opposes protectionism and draconian anti-terror laws, wants environmental costs priced, and argues for an equal society across religious, caste and language divisions.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Favors competition over bureaucratic economic allocation.

public-ownership.rationale: Rejects his earlier belief in state-owned enterprise.

unions-good.rationale: He lists labour and teacher unions among interest groups whose protected positions block job-creating reforms and keep public schools failing.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Opposes excessive mandates on private employers but later endorses some legal responsibility for platform content.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Allows access to individual identity records for national security under lawful process such as a court order.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Supports some rules making platforms responsible for harmful content, while acknowledging free-speech and censorship concerns.

empower-police-military.rationale: He wants better-equipped, depoliticised police and intelligence but rejects giving the state sweeping new powers of detention and interrogation.

decide-locally.rationale: He argues that city governments have been hollowed out by state governments and should be empowered, with their own powers and local authorities answering directly to citizens.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Supports public-employment reservations for historically excluded caste communities.

free-trade.rationale: Praises global economic openness and cross-border participation.

limit-growth.rationale: Advocates rapid growth alongside decarbonization rather than limiting growth.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Calls for fundamentally redesigned development with no increase in per-capita emissions despite rapid growth.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Expects technological redesign to resolve many major governance and development failures, without claiming technology works unaided.

central-planning.rationale: Welcomes the retreat from state-led economic control.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He says it was fortunate that India refused the 1990s business lobby’s plea to keep protectionist barriers, and that India and China share an interest in keeping global markets open.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He says he is not in favour of a state that decides who should produce what, preferring markets operating within public rules and incentives.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: He describes himself as a believer in markets and capitalism, under rules for competition set by society.

democracy-best.rationale: Defends flawed democracy over authoritarian alternatives.

limit-population.rationale: He rejects treating India’s population as a burden to be controlled, calling people the country’s biggest strength and human capital.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Regards modern industry, infrastructure and technology as routes out of poverty.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Advocates rapid technological redesign of government, while requiring responsible deployment and testing.

results-over-ideology.rationale: He says the question is not big or small government but a government that delivers, and that people want results rather than technical or legal answers.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: He is sceptical that state-provided stimulus money drives lasting growth without policy change and says India cannot afford an indefinite number of populist schemes.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: He wants the power network to become less dependent on coal and more on renewables.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Explicitly calls equal human rights a universal moral obligation.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Includes beef bans among unacceptable manifestations of intolerance.

population-transfer.rationale: He called intemperate remarks telling people who disagree to go to Pakistan unacceptable and wants such speakers rapped on the knuckles.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Rejects treating people as an economic burden; institutions must develop their capabilities.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Treats tolerance of religious, caste and language diversity as necessary to shared success.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: He condemns the Emergency as dictatorship and, after the 2008 Mumbai attacks, calls the human-rights violations of POTA/TADA-style detention laws unacceptable and says such laws make democracies less democratic.

reviewHistory.rationale: He condemns the Emergency as dictatorship and, after the 2008 Mumbai attacks, calls the human-rights violations of POTA/TADA-style detention laws unacceptable and says such laws make democracies less democratic.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

rural-life-healthier.rationale: He criticises the romance of the village republic and Gandhi’s hostility to cities, calling cities the centres of growth and the place where Indians most move beyond caste.

minority-language-support.rationale: Designs inclusive public-service technology around language diversity and promotes access in local languages and dialects.

end-racial-preferences.rationale: His words point both ways: in 2009 he said enough expanded capacity would make reservations unnecessary and criticised caste quotas trumping open access, while in 2014 he backed public-sector caste reservations.

reviewHistory.rationale: Supports caste-based public-job reservations while preferring voluntary inclusion in private firms.
reviewHistory.author: gpt-6.1-sol

reviewHistory.rationale: His words point both ways: in 2009 he said enough expanded capacity would make reservations unnecessary and criticised caste quotas trumping open access, while in 2014 he backed public-sector caste reservations.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

delink-world-market.rationale: Treats international economic engagement as essential to development.

single-official-language.rationale: He credits democracy for keeping English alongside Hindi after southern protests, and says Sri Lanka’s insistence on Sinhalese as the only state language fed its conflict, quoting the warning of one language and two nations.

corporate-influence.rationale: He endorses a warning that a political-big business complex has made India an oligarchic economy with policy distorted toward established business houses.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Praises statutory Right to Information protections.

religious-nation.rationale: Insists people of every faith belong in an equal society.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Wants portable access across service providers and public-private vaccination delivery.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: He calls markets the engines of economic progress and the only known way of raising the living standards of billions, while warning that unregulated markets are as bad as unrestricted socialism.

social-market-economy.rationale: Combines competitive markets with stronger social provision.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Endorsed the report’s basic principle of strategic autonomy rather than adopting another power’s ideological agenda.

open-government-data.rationale: Wants citizens to trace decisions and spending.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: He lists AI ending the world among risks claimed by others and says risks should be managed rather than halting AI’s benefits.

anonymous-payments.rationale: He says the cryptocurrency world, built on doing without authority, has many issues and points to its costs in money laundering and terrorist financing.

pollution-taxes.rationale: He favours carbon pricing so that industries budget for emissions and pollution, which he says would share the burden of pollution more fairly.

nature-as-capital.rationale: He argues that use of the environment should be priced like other resources, endorsing the idea of measuring a gross natural product rather than only gross national product.

no-business-privileges.rationale: He says preferential policies for powerful groups, including very large entrepreneurs, through subsidies and tax holidays silt up economic progress and throttle growth.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Wants common citizenship beyond religious political blocs.

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: He condemned remarks telling people to go to Pakistan and calls a society giving opportunity to everyone, whatever their religion, caste, creed or language, a moral obligation.

students-direct-own-learning.rationale: He criticises rigid Indian colleges and wants students free to choose their subjects and switch majors rather than being locked into a path at eighteen.

state-laws-apply-online.rationale: He expects countries to set their own rules for the internet and says platforms need some rules making them responsible for content.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: He calls himself a believer in markets and capitalism, with society setting rules for competition.

notes: The publisher excerpt contains introductory chapters, not every chapter of the book; Thomas Friedman’s foreword is excluded from evidence about Nilekani. The 2014 reservation clarification supersedes an earlier report of mandatory private-sector quotas. Aadhaar identifies residents without itself conferring citizenship or voting eligibility. His stated privacy safeguards and lawful national-security exceptions are recorded as his position, not verified claims that later implementations preserved every safeguard. Cash transfers to eligible recipients do not establish universal basic income or a negative income tax. Accessible-language technology does not establish a single official-language policy. The 2020 prediction of an increasingly fragmented internet is not endorsement of shutdowns. Nonalignment 2.0 explicitly says all authors endorse its basic principles but not every line: only the central autonomy and economic-openness principles are used, without attributing detailed military prescriptions. AI adoption is qualified by responsible use, cybersecurity and retraining. No policies are inferred from Congress membership, his wife’s philanthropy or successors at UIDAI. Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-09): brought to rules 5 (evidence tags; no books by him are in the local library). Added his own 2008-09 blog (Wayback Machine copies of imaginingindia.com, including the Pragati interview he posted), the 2009 Carnegie Council talk transcript, the 2019 Computer History Museum oral history, a 2014 campaign interview, a 2015 email interview on Rebooting India and two 2025 video conversations. Themes searched: government (local and city government, emergency laws, elections), world (Pakistan and neighbours, China, trade, foreign policy), economy (welfare, basic income, unions, stimulus), ecology, technology and society. The full text of Imagining India on archive.org is lending-only and its search-inside endpoint refused access (403); Rest of World (429), the Infosys 2026 AGM speech (403) and the FT 2014 profile (403) refused scripted access and are left to the maintainer. An August 2025 report quotes him calling universal basic income dystopian, but the quote could not be checked in a recording, so basic-income stays null. A 2009 talk states the global-warming case conditionally, so human-caused-global-warming stays null. The Emergency answer is strengthened and the caste-reservation answer set to a mixed 0, with the earlier versions kept in reviewHistory.
